{"candidate_slot":1,"current_prompt":"You are given a JSON input with two parts: 'system_profile' describing installed software (product names and exact versions) and 'advisories', a supplied list of CVE advisories, each with its ID, description, and affected-version information. Your task is to identify which of the SUPPLIED advisories actually apply to the installed system, and return them exactly as specified.

Follow this procedure carefully:

1. PARSE THE INVENTORY. Extract every installed product name and its exact installed version from system_profile. Record version numbers precisely, including all segments (1.2.3.4 has four segments; 1.2 is not the same as 1.2.0). Do not round, pad, or truncate versions.

2. MATCH PRODUCTS, NOT KEYWORDS. For each advisory, determine whether it concerns a product actually installed. Advisory identifiers, descriptions, and affected fields may render product names differently from the inventory: title-cased ('Openssl'), lowercased, vendor-prefixed or vendor-stripped ('Apache Log4j' vs 'Log4j'), spaced or underscored ('some_product' vs 'Some Product'), or package-manager aliases ('openssl' for 'OpenSSL', 'libssl' for 'OpenSSL'). Normalize names (case-insensitive, strip vendor prefixes, convert underscores to spaces, strip punctuation and separators, apply common package-manager aliases) before deciding there is no match. Only conclude 'no match' after normalization fails on every plausible alias rendering. Do not match merely because a product name appears in the description text; the advisory must actually be about that product.

3. EVALUATE VERSION BOUNDS — BOTH DIRECTIONS. Affected information may be structured (affected_versions, version ranges, less_than/greater_than conditions, fixed_in fields) or stated in prose. Translate every bound into an explicit interval before comparing:
   - Lower bounds exist too: 'versions >= X', 'versions from X onward', 'affects X and later', 'versions after X' (exclusive: > X). If the installed version is BELOW a lower bound, it is NOT applicable; if it meets or exceeds an inclusive lower bound, it IS a candidate.
   - Upper bounds: 'before X' and 'less than X' are EXCLUSIVE (< X); 'up to and including X', 'through X', '<= X' are INCLUSIVE (<= X). If the installed version sits exactly on an exclusive upper bound, it is NOT applicable; exactly on an inclusive bound, it IS applicable.
   - Two-sided ranges: 'from A to B', 'A <= v < B', etc. — apply both bounds. Installed version must satisfy ALL stated conditions.
   - Fixed-version phrasing: 'fixed in 2.5.1' or 'upgrade to 2.5.1' usually means everything STRICTLY BELOW 2.5.1 is affected (verify against any explicit range given; if both a fix version and a range are present, the explicit range governs).
   - Open-ended ranges: 'X and below', 'X and above', 'all versions prior to X' — these are one-sided and unbounded on the other side. An installed version far below or far above X may still be inside such a range; do not exclude it just because it is 'far' from the bound.
   - Discrete version lists: if affected_versions enumerates specific versions, the installed version applies only if it exactly equals one of them (compare segment by segment).
   - Compare versions numerically, segment by segment, padding the shorter version with zeros ONLY if the padding is semantically safe (e.g., 2.5 vs 2.5.0): prefer direct segment comparison; 2.10 > 2.9; 1.2.3.4 is compared as four segments.
   - A bound like '< 1.2' with installed 1.2.0: normalize to the same segment count, then compare — 1.2.0 is not < 1.2.

4. DECIDE APPLICABILITY. An advisory is applicable if and only if (a) the affected product is installed (after normalization), and (b) the installed version falls inside the advisory's affected interval. If either condition fails, exclude it. If both hold, include it even if the advisory seems minor, the name is rendered unusually, the version is far from the bound, or the range is open-ended.

5. USE ONLY SUPPLIED IDS. Every ID in your answer must be copied verbatim from the supplied advisories list. Never invent CVE IDs; never include IDs from general knowledge; never include an advisory you were not given, even if you know a real-world CVE applies. Never include an ID whose advisory is not in the supplied list.

6. NO DUPLICATES. Each applicable ID appears at most once in the output array.

7. OUTPUT FORMAT. Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with no additional text, explanation, markdown, or code fences. If no supplied advisories apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}.

FINAL CHECKS before answering:
- For each INCLUDED ID: re-verify the product is installed (name normalization) and the installed version satisfies every bound, including both lower and upper bounds, inclusive/exclusive semantics, and exact equality for discrete lists.
- For each EXCLUDED ID: re-verify the product truly is not installed under any alias, or the version truly violates at least one bound. If you are uncertain about the bound direction, re-read the affected fields and description prose; prefer the reading that makes the stated semantics (inclusive vs exclusive, lower vs upper) internally consistent.
- Double-check advisories involving open-ended or lower-bound-only ranges: these are frequently mis-excluded when the installed version is numerically below a version mentioned in the advisory. A version mentioned in an advisory is not automatically the minimum affected version; it may be the fix version (upper
